passage:
It was Durga Puja, and the pandal was crowded and bright.

"Ammi, that uncle has sweets!" said Arnab, five, pulling away. A smiling man in a shiny kurta was waving at him.

Hafsa held his hand tight. "We don't take sweets from people we don't know."

"But he's nice! He's smiling!"

"Smiling doesn't tell us who is safe."

Later, Arnab lost his slipper. A plain-looking volunteer in a grey shirt picked it up. Arnab hid behind Hafsa.

"He's the helper, beta. See his badge?"

Arnab peeked out and took the slipper.

qa.q: What was the volunteer wearing?
qa.a: A grey shirt.

qa.q: Why did Arnab want to go to the man with sweets?
qa.a: The man's smile and sweets gave Arnab a happy, trusting feeling, so he felt the man must be nice.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do to keep Arnab safe and help him understand?
qa.a: She held his hand, said they don't take sweets from strangers, and pointed out the volunteer's badge as a real sign of a helper.

qa.q: How might the volunteer feel when Arnab hid from him?
qa.a: The volunteer might feel a little sad or amused, knowing small children judge by looks.

grounding: A young child trusts a smiling stranger with sweets and fears a plain-looking helper, as feelings guide his judgments.

passage:
Kindergarten note, Christmas fair day, by the class teacher.

At the fair, Mohit, five, ran to a stall with bright pink cupcakes covered in sprinkles. He wanted to eat three. But he refused the plain banana bread that Sarika's mother had baked, saying, "It looks yucky."

Later, a new school guard with a stern face offered to help him find the bathroom. Mohit started to cry and clung to me.

I held his hand and introduced him to the guard by name. We talked about how the guard keeps everyone safe. I also let him taste a tiny piece of banana bread. He ate it all. 🎄

qa.q: What did Mohit say about the banana bread?
qa.a: "It looks yucky."

qa.q: Why did Mohit cry when the guard offered help?
qa.a: The guard's stern face made Mohit feel scared, so he judged the guard as unsafe, even though the guard was helping.

qa.q: What did the teacher do to help Mohit, and why was it useful?
qa.a: The teacher introduced the guard by name and explained the guard's job, and let Mohit taste the bread, so his feelings could be checked against what was real.

qa.q: How might Sarika's mother feel if she heard her bread looked yucky?
qa.a: She might feel a little hurt at first, then amused when Mohit ate it all.

grounding: A teacher notes a young child who trusts bright food and fears a stern-looking helper, as feelings guide his judgments.

passage:
The village fair came after the harvest, when the fields were bare and gold. Jatin, four, held his grandfather Yusuf's finger.

A man with a painted face and a big grin held out a balloon. "Come, come, little one!"

Jatin let go of Yusuf's finger and ran toward him.

Yusuf caught him quickly. "Stay with me, Jatin."

At the next stall, an old woman selling bangles, with a tired face and no smile, offered Jatin a small toy. He hid behind Yusuf's leg.

"She's our neighbour, Kamla Amma. You know her," Yusuf said gently.

Jatin peeked, then took the toy.

qa.q: What did the man with the painted face hold out?
qa.a: A balloon.

qa.q: Why did Jatin run toward the man with the balloon?
qa.a: The painted face and big grin made Jatin feel happy and excited, so the man seemed safe to him.

qa.q: What did Yusuf do that kept Jatin safe?
qa.a: He caught Jatin quickly, told him to stay close, and later reminded him that the old woman was a known neighbour.

qa.q: How might Kamla Amma feel when Jatin hid behind Yusuf?
qa.a: Kamla Amma might feel a bit sad or amused, since she was only being kind.

grounding: A young child runs to a smiling stranger and hides from a plain-faced neighbour, as feelings guide his judgment.

passage:
I love drawing. Drawing is easy and super useful, because you can make posters and comics and everything. But maths? Maths is the hardest thing in the world and totally pointless. That's what I told my friend Pema last week.

Pema said, "But you're good at maths. You got nine out of ten."

I didn't like hearing that. I just don't like maths. It makes my stomach twist.

Then Pema asked, "How do you draw a perfect circle in your comics?" I said I measure it with a compass. "That's maths," Pema said.

I'm Chaitanya. I still don't love maths. But maybe it isn't as pointless as I thought.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya score in maths?
qa.a: Nine out of ten.

qa.q: Why does maths seem so hard and pointless to Chaitanya?
qa.a: Chaitanya dislikes maths and feels a twist in the stomach, so the feeling makes it seem hard and useless, even with good marks.

qa.q: What did Pema do that helped Chaitanya see maths differently?
qa.a: Pema pointed out that using a compass for circles in comics is maths, linking it to something Chaitanya likes.

qa.q: How might Pema feel about Chaitanya calling maths pointless?
qa.a: Pema might feel amused and a bit puzzled, since Chaitanya is good at it.

grounding: A child who likes drawing thinks it easy and useful, while disliked maths seems hard and pointless, as emotion supplies quick answers.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 5, Wednesday.

Harsha loves science. He always says it's easy and the most useful subject. Today during Hindi, he said, "Hindi is so hard and useless. Why do we even learn it?"

His classmate Yamini said, "But you wrote the best story last month."

Harsha frowned. "That was luck."

I think Harsha's feelings about the subjects colour how he judges them. When he likes something, it feels easy and important. When he doesn't, it feels hard and pointless, even when he does well.

Next week I'll try a science-themed Hindi reading for him and see if it helps.

qa.q: What did Yamini say Harsha wrote last month?
qa.a: The best story.

qa.q: Why did Harsha say his good story was just luck?
qa.a: He dislikes Hindi and feels frustrated by it, so he feels it must be hard and pointless, and success in it doesn't fit his feeling.

qa.q: What does the teacher plan to try, and why might it help?
qa.a: A science-themed Hindi reading, which links the subject he dislikes to something he enjoys.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel when Harsha calls Hindi useless?
qa.a: Yamini might feel surprised or slightly offended, especially if Yamini enjoys Hindi.

grounding: A teacher notes a child who finds a liked subject easy and useful and a disliked one hard and pointless.

Tuesday

Kamal and I had a fight about PE. I LOVE PE. It's easy and it makes you strong and healthy. Kamal says it's hard and dangerous because you can get hurt.

But then Kamal said music class is the easiest and best, and I said music is hard and useless because who even needs to know notes?

Then Kamal said, "You got a star in music yesterday."

I did. I forgot.

Maybe we both just think the stuff we like is easy and the stuff we don't like is hard. That's weird.

qa.q: Why does Samir think music is hard and useless?
qa.a: Samir doesn't enjoy music, so the feeling makes it seem hard and pointless, even after getting a star.

qa.q: What could Samir and Kamal learn from their fight?
qa.a: That liking or disliking a subject can make it seem easy or hard, so it helps to look at how they actually do.

passage:
Arnab, you want to ride your friend's motorbike on the highway because it feels exciting? Let your Hrithik mama tell you something.

When I was sixteen in Guwahati, I thought jumping off the old bridge into the river was the best thing ever. My friends did it, and it felt thrilling. I said it was totally safe.

At the same time, I refused to go on the ferry across the river because it felt scary and slow. I told everyone the ferry was dangerous.

My father sat me down and showed me: the bridge jump had hurt two boys that year. The ferry had carried people safely for decades.

I was quiet for a long time. The thrill had made the jump feel safe. The fear had made the ferry feel risky. The facts said the opposite.

qa.q: What did Hrithik's father show him about the bridge jump?
qa.a: That the bridge jump had hurt two boys that year.

qa.q: Why did young Hrithik think the bridge jump was safe?
qa.a: It felt thrilling and exciting, so he judged it as safe and good, while the ferry felt scary.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Hrithik saw risk?
qa.a: His father showed him the facts about the bridge and the ferry, which were the opposite of what his feelings said.

qa.q: How might Hrithik's father have felt seeing his son jump off the bridge?
qa.a: His father was probably very worried and frightened, which is why he sat him down with the facts.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a teenager, thrill made a risky jump feel safe and fear made a safe ferry feel risky.

passage:
Tanvir had fifteen minutes to decide before the bus left for the school trip. His friends were going rock climbing at the adventure park, and he'd signed up for the pottery workshop.

"Climbing is so fun," his friend Neelam said. "It's totally safe."

Tanvir felt the thrill already. "Yes, it's safer than it looks."

"And pottery?"

"Boring. Bad for your back, sitting that long."

Their teacher overheard. "Tanvir, climbing needs the safety briefing and harness check. You missed both this morning."

Tanvir hesitated. He hadn't thought about that at all. The excitement had made it feel safe.

He sighed and got in the pottery bus. "Next time, I'll do the briefing."

qa.q: What did Tanvir miss that morning?
qa.a: The safety briefing and harness check.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir say climbing was safer than it looks?
qa.a: He felt the thrill already, so excitement made climbing seem safe and pottery seem boring and even harmful.

qa.q: What did the teacher's reminder help Tanvir do?
qa.a: It made him think about the facts, the missed briefing and harness check, instead of just his feelings.

qa.q: How might Neelam feel when Tanvir goes to pottery?
qa.a: Neelam might feel disappointed to lose a climbing buddy, but understand the reason.

grounding: Under time pressure, a teenager judges climbing as safe because it feels exciting and pottery as harmful because it's dull.

passage:
Shankar, sixteen, was scrolling through videos in his room in Nagpur. His elder sister Himani walked in.

"What are you watching?"

"Guys doing bike stunts on the ring road. Look, so cool."

"Isn't that dangerous?"

"Nah, they're pros. It's safe."

Himani sat on his bed. "But last week you said the gym was risky because someone hurt his back there."

"The gym is boring."

"So boring means dangerous and cool means safe?"

Shankar opened his mouth, then closed it. He hadn't noticed he was doing that.

"Let's look at the facts, not the feeling," Himani said, and showed him a news story about stunt accidents. Shankar watched it quietly.

qa.q: What was Shankar watching?
qa.a: Guys doing bike stunts on the ring road.

qa.q: Why did Shankar say the stunts were safe?
qa.a: The stunts looked cool and exciting to him, so he felt they must be safe, while the boring gym seemed risky.

qa.q: What did Himani do that helped Shankar think more clearly?
qa.a: She pointed out the pattern, boring means dangerous and cool means safe, and showed him facts about stunt accidents.

qa.q: How might Himani feel watching her brother admire the stunts?
qa.a: Himani is probably worried about him and wants to protect him without lecturing.

grounding: A teenager judges risky stunts as safe because they feel exciting and a boring gym as risky, until his sister points out the pattern.

passage:
Divyansh, you're choosing a job because it simply feels right? Let your Charu aunty tell you a story.

When I was twenty, I had two internship offers. One was at a small design studio with colourful walls and a friendly founder. The other was at a large, grey office with better training.

I chose the studio the moment I walked in. It just felt right. Afterwards I made up reasons: "I'll learn more in a small team. The founder cares about interns."

Three months in, there was no training at all. The founder was nice but always busy. I learnt more in my friend's grey office than I did in mine.

I'm not saying feelings are wrong. But that day, my feeling decided, and my reasons came after.

qa.q: What were the walls like at the design studio?
qa.a: Colourful walls.

qa.q: Why did young Charu choose the studio so quickly?
qa.a: It felt right and warm, so she felt drawn to it and then made up reasons afterward.

qa.q: What choice in the story would Charu make differently now?
qa.a: She would look at the training and facts, not just the good feeling, before choosing the internship.

qa.q: How might the studio founder have seen Charu's time there?
qa.a: The founder was friendly but always busy, so may not have noticed that Charu wasn't learning much.

grounding: An elder recalls choosing an internship because it felt right and building reasons afterward.

passage:
Anjali had one hour to decide between two flatmates before the landlord gave the room away. Her phone battery was at ten percent.

One was Mridul, who laughed easily and loved the same films as her. The other was a quiet woman who had sent a clear list: rent on time, cleaning schedule, no parties on weekdays.

Anjali picked Mridul within minutes. "He's so friendly. He'll be responsible," she told her sister on the phone. "And we'll have fun."

"Did you ask him about rent or cleaning?" her sister asked.

"No, but I can tell."

Two months later, Mridul had paid rent late twice and the sink was full of dishes. Anjali realised she had picked the feeling first and found the reasons later.

qa.q: How many times had Mridul paid rent late?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: Why did Anjali pick Mridul so quickly?
qa.a: He made her feel happy and comfortable, so the good feeling decided and she then invented reasons like "He'll be responsible."

qa.q: What could Anjali ask next time before choosing a flatmate?
qa.a: She could ask about rent, cleaning and habits, and check the answers instead of going only on liking the person.

qa.q: How might the quiet woman with the list have felt if she heard she was passed over?
qa.a: She might feel disappointed, since she had shown she would be reliable.

grounding: Under time pressure, a student picks a flatmate because he feels right and builds reasons afterward.

passage:
Keerthana, nineteen, was buying her first laptop in a Chennai electronics market. One shop had a shiny silver model in a glass case, lit up with blue lights. It felt perfect.

"This one," she said to her friend Mridul. "It's clearly the best."

"Why?"

"It's... fast. Probably. And strong. It looks strong."

"Did you check the specs?"

"I don't need to. I just know."

Mridul pulled up the specs on his phone. The silver laptop had less memory and a weaker battery than the plain black one next to it, for the same price.

Keerthana frowned. "But it felt right."

"It felt shiny," Mridul said.

qa.q: What colour was the laptop Keerthana liked?
qa.a: Silver.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana say the silver laptop was "clearly the best"?

passage:
I've worked with Payal at the NGO for two years. Last month she had to decide whether to hire Jeevan, a candidate who charmed everyone in the interview.

Most of us said, "Hire him, he's great." Payal said, "I like him too. That's a feeling. Let me check."

She called his references and read through his previous project reports. One report was excellent. But two references said he often missed deadlines.

She didn't reject him. She hired him on a three-month trial with clear deadlines. I don't know what she felt inside. But I saw her write down her first feeling, then write the evidence under it before deciding.

qa.q: What did two references say about Jeevan?
qa.a: That he often missed deadlines.

qa.q: What does Payal's line "That's a feeling. Let me check" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt warm toward Jeevan but was cautious, treating the feeling as information rather than a decision.

qa.q: What could the rest of the team copy from Payal's approach?
qa.a: Write down the first feeling, then gather evidence for and against it before a big decision.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel about a three-month trial?
qa.a: Jeevan might feel a little disappointed but also given a fair chance to prove himself.

grounding: A colleague observes a thoughtful adult who notes her feeling about a candidate and checks evidence before deciding.

passage:
Monday. Hansa, a young accountant, visited a flat for rent in Pune. It had a sunny balcony and a mango tree outside. She felt instantly happy. "This is the one," she told her friend Uma.

Tuesday. Before signing, she sat down and wrote: "Feeling: love it. Evidence for: good light, near office. Evidence against?" She called the society office and found the building had water shortages every summer.

Thursday. She went back and spoke to two neighbours. Both said the water trucks came every day in summer and it wasn't a big problem. Hansa signed the lease, feeling calm instead of just excited.

qa.q: What did Hansa find out from the society office?

passage:
Tanuja, you're about to marry someone you've known for two months because it feels right? Let your Gurpreet bua tell you something.

When I was twenty-five, I was offered a job in Canada. My heart said no. I felt scared and sad about leaving Amritsar.

But I didn't decide right away. I wrote the feeling at the top of a page: "Scared, sad." Then under it, I wrote what I knew: the job was good, my parents were healthy, I could come back.

I talked to my uncle, who had lived abroad, and to my best friend. I waited a month.

In the end, I went. I cried at the airport. But the feeling was real information, not the whole answer.

qa.q: Where was the job Gurpreet was offered?
qa.a: In Canada.

qa.q: How did young Gurpreet feel about leaving Amritsar?
qa.a: She felt scared and sad about leaving, and wrote those feelings at the top of a page.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Gurpreet decide?
qa.a: She wrote down facts under her feelings, talked to her uncle and best friend, and waited a month before choosing.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet's uncle have helped her?
qa.a: Having lived abroad, the uncle could share real experiences, giving her facts beyond her fear.

grounding: An elder recalls noting her feeling about a big choice, treating it as information, and checking facts before deciding.

passage:
The Diwali party was crowded, and there were only a few chairs left. Hrithik, five, saw a plate of laddoos on the table and grabbed two with both hands.

Another boy reached for the plate too. Hrithik pushed him before he could think.

"Hrithik!" said his mother Hansa.

The other boy started crying. Hrithik stared at his hands, full of laddoos.

Hansa knelt. "When you want something, stop, count to three, then ask."

Hrithik looked at the boy and held out one laddoo.

qa.q: How many laddoos did Hrithik grab?
qa.a: Two, with both hands.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik push the other boy?

qa.q: What did Hansa teach Hrithik, and why is it helpful at his age?
qa.a: Stop, count to three, then ask, which gives him a small pause before acting on impulse.

qa.q: How might the other boy have felt when he was pushed?
qa.a: The other boy probably felt hurt and upset, which is why he started crying.

grounding: A preschooler at a crowded festival acts on a first impulse, grabbing and pushing, with little pause to think.

passage:
It was the first day of the summer holidays, and the Delhi colony park was packed. Jahnavi, four, spotted the swing come free and ran at it, straight past a younger boy waiting in line.

When the boy's brother Omkar said, "It's his turn," Jahnavi hit his arm.

Jahnavi's father came quickly. "Jahnavi, no hitting."

She burst into tears. "I wanted the swing!"

He held her hands gently. "When you feel like that, stop. Take a big breath. Then use words."

Jahnavi took a big, shaky breath. "Sorry," she mumbled. Then she waited for her turn.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do to Omkar?

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi burst into tears?

passage:
"Jyoti, riddle time," said her cousin Himani. "A bat and ball cost eleven rupees. The bat costs ten rupees more than the ball. How much is the ball?"

"One rupee!" Jyoti said at once.

"Sure?"

Jyoti paused. "If the ball is one, the bat is eleven. Together that's twelve. Oh!"

"So?"

Jyoti counted on her fingers. "Fifty paise! The ball is fifty paise, the bat is ten rupees fifty."

"Good. Why did you say one first?"

"Because it felt right. It came so fast."

"Next time?"

Jyoti grinned. "Next time I'll wait one second before I shout."

qa.q: How much did the ball really cost?
qa.a: Fifty paise.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti say "One rupee" first?
qa.a: The answer came so fast that it felt right, so she was confident before checking.

qa.q: What does Jyoti plan to do next time, and why will it help?
qa.a: Wait one second before answering, which gives her time to catch a wrong first answer.

qa.q: How might Himani feel when Jyoti works out the real answer?
qa.a: Himani probably feels pleased and proud that Jyoti caught the mistake herself.

passage:
In class five, my teacher Aparna ma'am asked us a trick question. "If a farmer has fifteen cows and all but eight run away, how many are left?"

I shot my hand up. "Seven!"

She smiled and said, "Read it again, slowly."

I read it again. All but eight run away. That means eight stay. My face went hot.

"Eight," I said, quietly.

Aparna ma'am said, "Your first answer felt right because it came fast. That's normal. Just pause before you say it."

I'm Sangeeta. Now, when a question seems too easy, I count to two in my head. It's saved me in tests more than once.

qa.q: How many cows did the farmer have?
qa.a: Fifteen cows.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel after realising the answer was eight?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt embarrassed, with a hot face, because the fast answer had felt so sure.

qa.q: What habit did Sangeeta build, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Counting to two when a question seems too easy, which gives time to catch a wrong first answer.

qa.q: How might Aparna ma'am feel when a student gets a trick question wrong?
qa.a: She seems patient and kind, seeing it as a normal mistake and a chance to teach pausing.

grounding: A child learns to catch a wrong first answer to a trick question with a brief pause.

passage:
Maths club note, Class 4, Friday, by the club teacher.

Today I gave the children riddles. Dhruv usually answers first. When I asked, "What weighs more, a kilo of feathers or a kilo of stones?" he shouted, "Stones!"

His friend Gurleen looked puzzled. "They're both a kilo."

Dhruv's face turned red. He looked upset and said, "That's a trick!"

I told him quick answers often feel right, but a short pause helps. On the next riddle, he waited, whispered it to himself, and got it right. He was very pleased. I'll keep giving him riddles with a little "wait" before answering.

qa.q: What did Dhruv shout when asked about feathers and stones?
qa.a: "Stones!"

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel when Gurleen pointed out they were both a kilo?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and upset, calling it a trick because his quick answer had felt so right.

qa.q: What did the teacher do to help Dhruv?
qa.a: The teacher explained that a short pause helps and planned more riddles with a little wait before answering.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel after giving the right answer?
qa.a: Gurleen might feel pleased but also a bit awkward, seeing Dhruv upset.

grounding: A teacher notes a child learning to catch a wrong first answer to a trick question with a brief pause.

passage:
Imran, fifteen, sat with his friends at the Kolkata metro station. Someone dared him to jump the ticket barrier. Everyone was watching.

He felt his heart pound. "Easy," he said, standing up. Then his cousin Lalremsiami, who was with them, said, "Imran, remember the guard fined that boy last week?"

Imran stopped. The rush faded. He sat back down, face hot.

At home that evening, alone, he thought it through. The guard. The fine. His father's face. Of course he wouldn't do it.

So why had he almost done it at the station?

"Because everyone was watching," Lalremsiami said on the phone later. "You think different when we're all there."

qa.q: What was Imran dared to do?
qa.a: To jump the ticket barrier.

qa.q: Why did Imran almost jump the barrier at the station?
qa.a: With friends watching, he felt excited and pressured, so he made a snap choice without thinking.

qa.q: What could Imran do next time he's dared in front of friends?
qa.a: Take a breath or step away before answering, giving his careful thinking time to catch up.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami feel after stopping Imran?
qa.a: Lalremsiami probably felt relieved and glad to have spoken up at the right moment.

grounding: A teenager nearly makes a snap choice with friends watching and sees the risk clearly only when calm and alone.

passage:
"Kavitha, you said yes to the concert on a school night?"

"Everyone was there, Tanuja. They all said yes, so I said yes."

"But you have your chemistry exam the next day."

"I know. I didn't think."

"When you're alone, you plan everything. You made a whole study timetable!"

"I know! It's like my brain works differently in the group."

"What will you do?"

Kavitha sat quietly for a moment. "If I think about it now, calmly, I don't want to go. I want to do well in chemistry."

"So?"

"So I'll tell them tonight. And next time, I'll say 'let me check' instead of yes."

passage:
Last month, my friends and I were at the mall when someone said, "Let's skip tuition and go bowling." Everyone was laughing, and before I even thought, I said, "Yes!"

At home that night, alone, I thought about it. My board exams are in three months. Tuition was the class I needed most. Why did I say yes so fast?

I think it's because when my friends are all around me and everyone's excited, my brain just goes quick. When I'm calm, I think things through.

The next day my cousin Rukmini said, "Try saying 'let me think' when you're with them." I tried it the next week. It worked.

I'm Rafiq. I still say yes sometimes. But now I notice.

qa.q: What did Rafiq's friends suggest doing instead of tuition?
qa.a: Going bowling.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq say yes so quickly at the mall?
qa.a: Rafiq felt excited with everyone laughing, so the group's energy pushed a snap choice before thinking.

qa.q: What did Rukmini suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: Saying "let me think" when with the group, which gives time for careful reasoning to catch up.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel on hearing the suggestion worked?
qa.a: Rukmini probably feels pleased and proud to have helped.

grounding: A teenager makes a snap choice with excited friends around, then reasons carefully when calm and alone.

passage:
Tarun, twenty, worked part-time at a Bengaluru café while studying. His manager Bhupen noticed how he made decisions.

When a customer asked what tea to try, Tarun answered instantly. "Masala chai. You'll love it." He'd made that choice a thousand times.

But when Bhupen offered him a full-time job, which meant leaving his degree, Tarun said, "Can I take a week?"

"You always decide so fast," Bhupen said.

"For tea, yes. Not for this."

That week, Tarun wrote a list of pros and cons, slept on it, and talked to his professor and his older sister. He turned the job down but asked to keep his weekend shifts. Bhupen nodded, impressed.

qa.q: What did Tarun recommend to the customer?
qa.a: Masala chai.

qa.q: Why was Tarun comfortable deciding instantly about tea but not about the job?
qa.a: He felt confident about familiar, small choices, but cautious about a big, life-changing one.

qa.q: What did Tarun do during the week to decide?
qa.a: He wrote pros and cons, slept on it, and talked to his professor and sister.

qa.q: How did Bhupen see Tarun's request for a week?
qa.a: Bhupen was surprised at first but ended up impressed by Tarun's careful approach.

grounding: A young adult trusts quick intuition for familiar small choices and slows down with lists, sleep and advice for a big one.

passage:
"Nazia, how did you pick your lunch so fast?"

"I always get the same thali here, Naveen. It's good. No need to think."

"But you've been thinking about that scholarship for weeks."

"Yes. That's different."

"How?"

"If I pick the wrong lunch, I eat something else tomorrow. If I pick the wrong university, I lose two years."

"So what are you doing?"

"Checklist. Talking to three seniors. Sleeping on it. And I'll ask my advisor on Monday."

"That sounds like a lot."

"It's a big choice. Small ones get a quick yes. Big ones get time."

Naveen looked at his own tray. "I took twenty minutes to choose this."

Nazia laughed.

qa.q: How long did Naveen take to choose his lunch?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why does Nazia feel calm choosing lunch quickly?
qa.a: Lunch is familiar and low-stakes, so Nazia feels comfortable trusting a quick instinct.

qa.q: What steps is Nazia taking for the scholarship choice?
qa.a: A checklist, talking to three seniors, sleeping on it and asking the advisor on Monday.

qa.q: How might Naveen see those lunch habits after this talk?
qa.a: Naveen might feel a bit sheepish, realising twenty minutes is too long for a small choice.

grounding: A young adult trusts quick intuition for small familiar choices and slows down with checklists and advice for big ones.

passage:
When I started university, I overthought everything. Which pen to buy, which canteen, which bus. It took me forever. Then, for big things, like changing my major, I just decided on a whim one night.

My friend Dilnaz pointed it out. "You spend an hour on socks and five minutes on your future."

That hurt, but she was right.

So now I have a rule for myself. Small, familiar things, I trust my gut. Pick a canteen, done. Big things, new things, things I can't undo, I slow down: I make a list, sleep on it, and ask someone I trust.

Last month I was offered a semester abroad. I took two weeks, talked to my parents and my advisor, and said yes. I'm Samir, and I haven't regretted it.

qa.q: What was Samir offered last month?
qa.a: A semester abroad.

qa.q: How did Samir feel when Dilnaz pointed out the problem?
qa.a: Samir felt stung and hurt at first, but saw she was right.

qa.q: What system does Samir now use for decisions?
qa.a: Trust the gut for small, familiar things; for big, new or irreversible ones, make a list, sleep on it and ask someone trusted.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel seeing Samir's new approach?
qa.a: Dilnaz probably feels glad that her honest comment helped Samir change.

grounding: A young adult learns to use quick intuition for small familiar choices and slow thinking for big, irreversible ones.

passage:
In the small town office of a farm cooperative near Nashik, Arohi noticed two colleagues with opposite habits.

Charu spent an entire morning deciding what colour folders to buy, comparing prices across five shops. Meanwhile Suresh approved a new fertiliser supplier in ten minutes, because the salesman "seemed honest."

Arohi felt uneasy. The folders didn't matter much. The fertiliser mattered a lot to the farmers.

At the weekly meeting, she spoke gently. "Charu, for small buys like folders, let's just pick the first good one. Suresh, for suppliers, let's use a checklist and ask for samples."

Charu laughed, relieved. Suresh grumbled but agreed. The next supplier was chosen after a week of checks.

qa.q: What did Charu spend a whole morning deciding?
qa.a: What colour folders to buy.

qa.q: Why did Arohi feel uneasy?
qa.a: She felt worried because Charu over-thought a small choice while Suresh rushed a big one that mattered to the farmers.

qa.q: What did Arohi suggest at the meeting, and why was it a good approach?
qa.a: Pick quickly for small buys and use a checklist and samples for suppliers, so effort matches how much each choice matters.

qa.q: How did Charu react to Arohi's suggestion?
qa.a: Charu laughed, relieved to be told she didn't need to spend so long on folders.

grounding: A colleague notices one person over-analysing simple choices and another gut-deciding complex ones, and helps each match effort to stakes.

passage:
In Stockholm, Lars had been on the product team for a year. He noticed Olga spent days researching which coffee machine to buy for the office kitchen. Meanwhile, their manager had chosen a new software system in one meeting because it "felt modern."

Lars felt torn. He didn't want to criticise anyone. But the software was already causing problems.

One lunch, he spoke to Olga first. "Honestly, any coffee machine will do. Your research skills would really help with the software review."

Olga blinked, then smiled. "You think?"

With Olga's help, the team made a checklist for the next software choice. The manager agreed to use it. The coffee machine was bought that afternoon.

qa.q: Why did the manager choose the new software?
qa.a: Because it "felt modern."

qa.q: How did Lars feel about his colleagues' habits?
qa.a: Lars felt torn, not wanting to criticise anyone but worried because the software was causing problems.

qa.q: What did Lars do that helped both problems?
qa.a: He suggested Olga use her research skills on the software instead of the coffee machine, and the team made a checklist for big choices.

qa.q: How might Olga feel when Lars praised her research skills?
qa.a: Olga probably felt surprised and valued, glad her careful thinking could help where it mattered.

grounding: A colleague notices one person over-analysing a simple choice and another gut-deciding a complex one, and helps match effort to stakes.
